subject: Biotechnology
title: The He Jiankui Scandal
description: A 60-second lesson on The He Jiankui Scandal.

hook.text: In 2018 He Jiankui edited human embryos with CRISPR — creating the world's first gene-edited babies. The world was horrified.

buildup.text: He targeted CCR5 to create HIV resistance — but the edits were mosaic, incomplete, and of questionable medical necessity.

discovery.text: The scientific community condemned the experiment — consent was inadequate, risks were unknown, and oversight was absent.

twist.text: He Jiankui was sentenced to three years in prison — but the edited children, Lulu and Nana, carry modified genes for life.

climax.text: The WHO established a global registry for gene editing research — the scandal accelerated international governance efforts.

punchline.text: One rogue experiment changed everything — He Jiankui showed why bioethics matters.

quiz.question: What were the main ethical violations in the He Jiankui experiment?
options: He used an outdated gene editing technology
Inadequate consent, unnecessary medical intervention, mosaic edits with unknown risks, and no proper oversight
He conducted the experiment in a country where CRISPR was illegal

details.summary: In 2018, Chinese scientist He Jiankui shocked the world by announcing he had created the first gene-edited babies using CRISPR, targeting CCR5 to confer HIV resistance. The experiment violated ethical norms, lacked proper oversight, and resulted in his imprisonment.
details.whyItMatters: The He Jiankui scandal exposed gaps in international governance of human germline editing. It demonstrated that existing guidelines were insufficient to prevent rogue experiments and catalyzed urgent global efforts to establish enforceable oversight.
takeaways: He Jiankui created CRISPR-edited twin girls in 2018 without proper oversight
The experiment had no medical justification and exposed the children to unknown risks
The scandal accelerated international efforts to govern human germline editing

faq.question: What exactly did He Jiankui do?
faq.answer: He used CRISPR to disable the CCR5 gene in human embryos, which were then implanted and carried to term. The twins, Lulu and Nana, were born with edits that were mosaic and off-target, meaning the modification was incomplete and potentially harmful.

faq.question: Why was the experiment considered unethical?
faq.answer: The procedure had no clear medical necessity since the father's HIV was controlled by medication. Informed consent was inadequate. The editing was imprecise with off-target mutations. It violated Chinese regulations and international consensus against heritable human genome editing.
